info.bio:
Terius Youngdell Nash (14 de junio, 1981), conocido bajo su nombre artístico como The-Dream, es un cantante, escritor y productor de R&B estadounidense. Nació en Carolina del Norte, pero se mudó a Atlanta tras morir su madre a la edad de 35 años, donde fue criado por su abuelo.

Conoció al productor Laney Stewart en 2001, que le ayudó a firmar un acuerdo de publicación. Pasó dos años trabajando en el segundo álbum de Nivea "Complicated"

podcast.title: Brian Cox's Parallel Careers
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, Brian Cox was a keyboardist in the electro-pop band Dream while simultaneously pursuing his PhD in physics. He is now Professor Brian Cox, a prominent British scientist involved with the Large Hadron Collider in Switzerland. "Back in the early 90s, Brian played keyboards in an electro pop band called Dream."

xref.title: Formation as All-Electronic Band (1967)
xref.body: Tangerine Dream was formed in 1967 as an all-electronic band, exploring the new sonic possibilities opened up by electronic instruments and synthesizers, particularly in West Germany where much of this experimentation occurred. "In 1967, the all electronic band Tangerine Dream was formed."

xref.title: Last Concert and Tour Plans (October 1977)
xref.body: The next leg of their tour commenced on October 13 in Statesboro, Georgia. The band had ambitious plans to play Madison Square Garden several weeks later, a long-held dream. Their final performance before the crash was on October 19, 1977, at the Greenville Memorial Auditorium in Greenville, South Carolina. "The next leg of the tour began on October 13th in statesboro, Georgia, and would eventually see the band realize their dreams by playing Madison Square Garden several weeks down the road."

xref.title: Drummer Audition (1987)
xref.body: In 1987, Dave Grohl discovered a notice at a music store indicating Scream was seeking a new drummer. He contacted the band, auditioned, and secured the position, which he considered his "dream gig," by the end of that month, replacing their long-time drummer. "He tore the note down, contacted the band, auditioned, and got what he thought was his dream gig by the end of that month."

xref.title: "All a Dream" Series Finale (1997)
xref.body: The final episode, aired on May 20, 1997, concluded with Barr delivering a voiceover revealing that the entire ninth season was a fantasy of her depressed character. The lottery win had not happened, and Dan had actually died from the heart attack he suffered at the end of season 8. Barr viewed this ending as representing her "total control" over the show, and the rest of the cast was unaware of this game-changing twist. "For Bar, this last episode represented her total control over the show."

xref.title: Dave Williams' Death on Tour (2002)
xref.body: On August 14, 2002, during Ozzfest, Drowning Pool's lead singer Dave Williams was found dead in his bunk on the tour bus, having died in his sleep. His death was attributed to cardiomyopathy, a disorder affecting the heart muscle often caused by viral infections or high blood pressure, thus determined to be from natural causes. The band later released a memorial DVD, with proceeds directed towards achieving Williams' dream of buying his parents a house. "He died of something called cardiomyopathy, a disorder that affects the heart muscle caused by things like viral infections or high blood pressure."

xref.title: "Siamese Dream" Cover Models Reunion
xref.body: The two young girls featured on *The Smashing Pumpkins'* *Siamese Dream* album cover, Ali Langer and Los Angeles Roberts, were child models who met for the first time at the photoshoot in Los Angeles. They are not Siamese twins, as the title might imply. In 2018, Langer and Roberts, now a nurse and an IT professional respectively, reunited to help promote a reformed Smashing Pumpkins and their tour. It has been confirmed that one-time Smashing Pumpkins bassist Nicole Fiorentino is not one of the girls on the cover, despite a claim she made that even fooled Billy Corgan. "In 2018, Ali and Los Angeles got back together to help promote a reformed smashing pumpkins and a tour."

xref.title: Big Muff as Core Sound
xref.body: The Smashing Pumpkins' existence and distinctive sound are attributed to a specific model of the Big Muff pedal. Electroharmonix even sold a custom orange-painted version described as "all the guitars on Simee's Dream in a box," a clear reference to the band's influential use of the pedal. "And there would not have been a smashing pumpkins if not for a specific model of Big Muff."

xref.title: Dream Machine Connection Myth
xref.body: A cult-like organization called "Friends Understanding Kurt" suggests that Kurt Cobain's death in 1994 was linked to his use of a "dream machine," a trance-inducing device invented by William Burroughs. After their 1992 collaboration, Burroughs was reportedly pleased and told Kurt about the machine, even introducing him to builder Dave Woodward in San Francisco. Kurt immediately ordered one, but Courtney Love, sensing its danger, tried to prevent its delivery. According to "Friends Understanding Kurt," Cobain used the machine for up to 72 hours at a time, and it was found just 20 feet from his body on April 8, 1994, though neither police nor the coroner investigated this connection. "The machine was found just 20 feet away from his dead body on April 8, 1994. Neither the police, nor the corner investigated the connection."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Dream Machine Invention
xref.body: William Burroughs invented a trance-inducing device called a "dream machine," which consists of a cylinder with an internal light source that rotates, causing the light to flash exactly 10.56 times per second. The theory is that staring at these flashes induces a trance-like state, and in the 1960s, several experimenters with these machines allegedly committed suicide. "The machine consists of a cylinder with a light source inside. When he switched on the cylinder rotates, causing the light to flash at a rate of exactly 10.56 times per second."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Dream Machine Recommendation to Kurt Cobain
xref.body: After their 1992 collaboration on "The Priest, they called him," William Burroughs was so pleased that he told Kurt Cobain about his invention, the "dream machine." He then connected Cobain with Dave Woodward, a builder in San Francisco who created these machines for special clients, leading to Cobain ordering one immediately. "Burroughs was apparently so pleased with how this recording turned out that he told Kurt about the dream machine. He even fixed him up with a guy in San Francisco named Dave Woodward who built machines for special clients."

xref.title: Drums on "Dream Weaver" (Gary Wright)
xref.body: The human drums featured on Gary Wright's song "Dream Weaver" were played by Art Wood, distinguishing them from the pure synthesizer elements found elsewhere on the record. "The else on that record is pure synthesizer, but the drums, that's a human, Art Wood."

xref.title: Early German Electronic Musicians
xref.body: Tangerine Dream was among the German groups that began creating electronic music in the early 1970s, seeking to establish a unique musical identity separate from the prevailing British and American rock and roll. This development was significantly aided by the experimental electronic studio built by West German Radio, which had exposed German musicians to electronic sounds for nearly two decades. "There were groups like Cannes and Tangerine Dream, and most important of all, Kraftwerk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Life Struggles
xref.body: Chester Bennington came from a broken home and struggled with substance abuse early in his life, reportedly spending money earned at Burger King on "Coke and Crystal meth." His primary motivation during this difficult period was his dream of becoming a rock star. "He was from a broken home. He spent the money he made at Burger King on Coke and Crystal meth."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Genre Fluidity and Influences
xref.body: Her music has shifted across many styles, including pop, rock, dream pop, psych, trip pop, and trap. Listeners can discern the "ghost" of iconic vocalists like Nina Simone, Frank Sinatra, Billie Holiday, and various torch singers in her sound. "If you close your eyes, you can hear the ghost of Nina Simone, Frank Sinatra, Billie Holiday, and any number of torch singers."

xref.title: German Electronic Music Pioneers
xref.body: Tangerine Dream was part of a movement of German (specifically West German) artists in the 1960s who sought to create a distinct musical identity by focusing on electronic sounds, rather than imitating American or British styles. "They had names like Tangerine Dream and Amundool."

xref.title: Inspiration for "TVC-15"
xref.body: Iggy Pop was involved in a dream or drug-induced hallucination with David Bowie that served as the inspiration for Bowie's song "TVC-15." "It was inspired by a dream, more likely a drug-induced hallucination with his friend, Ike Pop, where an unidentified girlfriend was eaten by a holographic television, model number, TVC-15."

xref.title: Legacy of the Marshall Stack – Drummer Invented Guitar Icon
xref.body: Jim Marshall, a drummer by profession and an engineer by training, conceived, invented, manufactured, and marketed the renowned Marshall amplifier and the iconic Marshall stack. This gear became the "dream gear for millions of guitar players around the world," solidifying his legacy as an inventor. "Did I mention that Jim's last name is Marshall? Yeah, the famous Marshall amplifier the famous Marshall stack the dream gear for millions of guitar players around the world Was conceived invented manufactured and marketed by a drummer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Leon Wilkeson's Dream
xref.body: After the crash, severely injured Leon Wilkeson recounted a dream where he spent time on a cloud-shaped log conversing with Ronnie Van Zant and Duane Allman of The Allman Brothers, who had died in a motorcycle crash six years earlier. In the dream, Ronnie told him, "boy, get yourself out of here. It's not your time yet." "He later recounted that he dreamed spending time on a cloud-shaped log talking with Ronnie Van Zant and Duane Alman of the Alman Brothers, who had died in a motorcycle crash six years earlier."

xref.title: MS Diagnosis and Career Shift
xref.body: Aaron was diagnosed with MS, which posed a significant challenge. At 24, he faced the difficult decision of leaving a stable, well-paying job with benefits at Chrysler to pursue his dream of being a drummer, a choice heavily influenced by his personal struggles at the time. This decision marked a "huge rebirth" for both him and the band. "Well, Aaron had been diagnosed with MS, which obviously threw us all in for a loop. ... And for me, at that time, in my life, I had to make the decision of staying at the good job that paid well and had benefits. ... But I was really just chasing this dream of being a drummer. And it just meant so much more to me because I was going through so much hard stuff in my life at that point. So, yeah, it was a huge rebirth for me personally and the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Physicist and Academic
xref.body: While playing keyboards for the dance act D:Ream (referred to as "Dream" in the transcript), Brian Cox studied physics at the University of Manchester. After the band ended in 1997, he continued his education, earning a doctorate in philosophy and working in high-energy particle physics, including at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in Switzerland. "When he was playing keyboards with them, he studied physics at the University of Manchester."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pre-flight Fears Among Band Members
xref.body: Several individuals associated with Leonard Skinnerd harbored significant fears about taking the fateful flight. Keyboardist Billy Powell's wife begged him not to board the plane, while backup singer Cassie Gaines, Steve Gaines' sister, initially wanted to travel with the equipment truck but was persuaded to fly. Guitarist Gary Rossington was "scared out of his mind," and backup singer JoJo Billingsley had a dream the night before that the plane crashed. "Keyboardist Billy Powell remembers his wife begging him not to get on the plane. Cassie Gaines, sister of Steve, wanted to ride with the band's equipment truck but was persuaded to fly."

xref.title: Travis Barker's Accessory Companies
xref.body: Travis Barker, the drummer for Blink-182, has established himself in the fashion accessory market. He owns a belt buckle company named American Dream and a shoe company known as DC Shoes, showcasing his involvement in the business side of youth culture fashion. "Travis Barker of Blink 182 has a hot belt buckle company called American Dream and a shoe company called DC Shoes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unfulfilled Dream of Being a Record Producer
xref.body: In high school, David Botrell aspired to be a record producer, driven by his love for music. However, he faced rejection from schools due to his lack of a portfolio at 18 and insufficient musical adeptness beyond being a "pretty good drummer" and having "seven years of accordion lessons." "I had the notion that I was going to be a record producer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Velvet Undergrounder Sound
xref.body: Based out of Cambridge, Galaxy 500 contributed to the shoegaze sound with their "Velvet Undergrounder sounds" and "wavy dream pop." Their music was described as mellow, featuring "crests and troughs" and introspective lyrics, aligning with the atmospheric and reflective qualities of shoegaze. "That made it nicely with the velvet undergrounder sounds of Galaxy 500, a mellow band based out of neighboring Cambridge, who specialized in sort of a wavy dream pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
